text: June the twenty-third, seventeen fifty-seven. Near the village of Plassey, in Bengal, about three thousand Company soldiers face roughly fifty thousand.
By sunset, the small army has won. But this battle was decided before a single shot was fired.
This is Siraj ud-Daulah, the young Nawab, or ruler, of Bengal. He took the throne only a year earlier, at twenty-three.
And this is Mir Jafar, a commander of his army. He has a secret.
Robert Clive of the East India Company has made him a deal. Turn on the Nawab, and the Company will make you Nawab instead.
In return, Mir Jafar promises the Company a fortune.
At eight in the morning, the guns open fire. For hours, cannon smoke drifts across the mango grove.
Then a heavy monsoon storm. The British throw tarpaulins over their gunpowder. The Nawab's powder is soaked, and his guns slow down.
Through it all, Mir Jafar's troops stand still. Thousands of men on the Nawab's side, who never join the fight.
Siraj flees on a camel, and the Company takes the field. Its losses are tiny. Twenty-two killed, though some records say twenty-seven.
Mir Jafar gets his throne. But the real power now sits with the Company. Within eight years, it is collecting Bengal's taxes itself.
So who really won at Plassey? The men who fought, or the man who stood still? Tell us in the comments.
